name: Palomino

lines.s10: Palomino is the plain white grape that becomes dry Sherry, from pale, salty Fino to dark, walnut scented Oloroso.
lines.s20: Palomino is the white grape of dry Sherry, grown on chalk around Jerez in southern Spain. It is mild by itself, and the cellar turns it into Fino, pale and salty under a film of yeast, or Oloroso, dark and nutty from years in air.
lines.s45: Palomino says very little on its own, and that is why Sherry is made from it. It grows on white chalk around Jerez, in the far south of Spain. The young wine is mild: green apple, a little almond, soft acidity. Then the cellar takes over. Aged under a film of yeast called flor it becomes Fino, pale and bone dry with a salty tang. Aged in air it becomes Oloroso, dark and full of walnut. Pour a cold Fino with olives, almonds or fried fish. Nearly every bottle is a blend of many years, drawn from a stack of casks called a solera.
lines.sale: Palomino becomes Fino, bone dry and salty, with almond and fresh bread, and a cold glass of it makes you hungry. I would pour it before dinner with olives and almonds, and bring an Amontillado when the turtle soup arrives.

glass.lead: As Fino, almond, bread dough and green apple with a salty tang, bone dry and light; as Oloroso, walnut, tobacco leaf and old leather.

ladder.where: Tenerife's high volcanic slopes, as Listán Blanco
The chalk hills of Jerez and Sanlúcar

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low. As Fino, light bodied, with alcohol a little above a table wine's; as Oloroso, full bodied and high in alcohol. Traditionally fortified.

home.home: Jerez, in Andalusia, on albariza, a white chalk that holds the winter rain through a rainless summer. The grape is picked early and fermented dry, then traditionally fortified. Under flor it becomes Fino, or Manzanilla at Sanlúcar; in air, Oloroso; Amontillado has known both. Most are blended down through the casks of a solera.
home.abroad: On the Canary Islands it is Listán Blanco, and on Tenerife's volcanic slopes it gives dry, smoky table wines. Inland Spain long grew it for volume, from Rueda to Galicia.

service.temp: 43 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, for Fino and Manzanilla; Amontillado and Oloroso cool, not cold.
service.glass: A copita or a small tulip; a white wine glass shows a Fino well.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary. Keep an open Fino in the fridge and finish it within days.
service.age: Bottled ready to drink. Pour Fino and Manzanilla young and fresh; Amontillado and Oloroso keep for years.

with.dish: Olives, salted almonds and cured ham
with.why: a cold Fino echoes the salt and the almond
Fino or Manzanilla, dry and salty, cuts the frying
a dry Amontillado suits a rich soup or consommé
the hazelnut of an Amontillado meets the roast
Oloroso has the weight and the walnut depth

labels.means: Aged under flor, the veil of yeast: pale and bone dry, with almond and bread dough.
A Fino style aged only in the sea air of Sanlúcar de Barrameda: lighter and saltier.
Begun under flor and finished in air: amber and dry, with hazelnut.
Aged in air from the start: dark, dry and full, with walnut and leather.
The grape's name on the Canary Islands, where it makes dry table wines.

guest.a: No. Most Sherry made from Palomino is bone dry: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado and Oloroso. The sweet ones are sweetened blends such as Cream, or wines of sun dried Pedro Ximénez.
A film of yeast that grows on the surface of the wine in the cask. It keeps the air off, so a Fino stays pale and fresh, and it gives the taste of almond and bread dough.

guest.q: How long will an open bottle keep?
guest.a: A Fino or Manzanilla keeps a few days in the fridge, so treat it like a white wine. An Amontillado or Oloroso has already lived with air and keeps for weeks.

compare.tell: Pedro Ximénez is the sweet one, black and syrupy from sun dried grapes, all raisin and fig; Palomino makes the dry Sherries, from pale Fino to dark Oloroso.
Savagnin, as vin jaune, also ages under a veil of yeast, but it is unfortified and sharply acid, with walnut and curry; Palomino, as Fino, is lighter, softer and saltier.

profile.st: Pale straw as Fino to mahogany as Oloroso · Body light to full · Acid low · Alcohol raised, traditionally by fortification · Bone dry
profile.fruit: Green apple when young, bruised apple under flor; little fruit of its own, which is what the cellar wants
profile.other: Almond, bread dough and sea brine under flor; hazelnut and tobacco leaf in Amontillado; walnut and old leather in Oloroso
profile.tell: A plain, low acid base that the cellar defines: almond and brine under flor, walnut in air, and the warmth of a wine traditionally fortified
profile.regions: Jerez, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María; the Canary Islands as Listán Blanco; Rueda and Galicia in small part
profile.confuse: Savagnin as vin jaune is unfortified and far higher in acidity, with walnut and curry; Pedro Ximénez is black, sweet and raisined

cards.front: Palomino: where is home, and what is the white soil called?
cards.back: Jerez, in Andalusia, with Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. The soil is albariza, a white chalky marl that holds winter rain through the dry summer.

cards.front: What does Palomino become under flor, and what in air?
cards.back: Under flor, the veil of yeast, it becomes Fino, or Manzanilla at Sanlúcar: pale and bone dry. Aged in air it becomes Oloroso: dark and dry, with walnut. Amontillado has had both.

cards.front: What is Palomino called on the Canary Islands, and what does it make?
cards.back: Listán Blanco. On volcanic soils, above all on Tenerife, it makes dry, unfortified whites with a smoky, flinty edge.

questions.q: A guest wants a bone dry Sherry, served cold, with olives and fried fish before dinner. Which style do you pour?
questions.exp: Fino is Palomino aged under flor: pale, bone dry and salty, served cold as an aperitif. Oloroso is dry too, but dark and full and served cool, and Cream is sweetened.

questions.q: A blind wine is pale straw, bone dry and light, with almond, bread dough, green apple and a salty tang, low acidity and a warmth of alcohol above a table wine's. Which is it?
questions.exp: Almond, bread dough and brine with low acidity and added strength mark a Fino. Vin jaune also ages under a veil of yeast, but it is unfortified and sharply acid, with walnut and curry.

questions.q: A guest asks why her Fino is pale and fresh while the Oloroso beside it is brown, though both are Palomino. What made the difference?
opts: Fino aged under flor, Oloroso in contact with air
Fino is from white grapes, Oloroso from black
Oloroso had caramel added for colour
Fino is bottled within a year of the harvest
questions.exp: Flor, a veil of yeast, shields a Fino from oxygen, so it stays pale. Oloroso is traditionally fortified higher, which keeps flor away, and years in air turn it brown, with walnut.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Jerez, with the Canary Islands (Listán Blanco) and inland Spain given as abroad.

A thin grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES. It agrees with the Régionale row (warm, low acidity, almond and bruised apple, a neutral base whose character comes from flor and the solera).

No Codex record is contradicted. The Jerez record supplied albariza, the early harvest, flor, the two paths of ageing, Manzanilla as a place, the solera and the service of each style; the Canary Islands record supplied Listán Blanco and its smoky, flinty whites; the Rueda, Bierzo and Galicia records the plantings for volume.

Fortification is written as traditional, never as a rule: the Codex records that unfortified dry Sherry has been allowed since August 2025. Nearly every bottle and most are blended leave room for the rare single vintage Sherry.
Alcohol is given in words, as the brief asks: a little above a table wine's for Fino, high for Oloroso.

The ladder sets Tenerife's high slopes on the moderate rung beside Jerez on the warm one; its notes are the Codex's own for each place. Crushed chalk and fresh yeast among the notes of a Fino are a taster's reading; no source read lists them by name.
Left out for want of a source read in this session: the plantings in South Africa, California and Australia, and the old belief that the grape is named for a knight of the thirteenth century.
The turtle soup, with a dry Amontillado, is the one dish from the Creole table; the regulatory council's own guide sets Amontillado beside soups and consommés.
Savagnin, the second compare, has no fragment yet; the tell agrees with the reviewed profile of Savagnin (Fino is fortified and softer in acid).
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. Listán Blanco as the same vine, the service of each style and how long an open bottle keeps were confirmed; the rest stands on the Codex's Jerez record.
changed: compare, the Savagnin tell: Fino is lighter now reads Palomino, as Fino, is lighter, so that the tell names both grapes.
profile.st: Alcohol raised by fortification now reads Alcohol raised, traditionally by fortification. The Codex records that dry Sherry may reach its strength with no added spirit since August 2025.
profile.tell: with the warmth of added grape spirit now reads and the warmth of a wine traditionally fortified, for the same reason.
open: The plantings in South Africa, California and Australia stay out, as the author left them, for want of a source read.
The ladder sets a table wine of Tenerife beside a Fino of Jerez: honest of each place, though the two rungs are two wines as much as two climates.
Turtle soup with a dry Amontillado stands on the Codex's own line (Amontillado with consommé); the council's guide the author cites was not read in this session.
